title: Mental Health and the Brain
bigQuestion: How has our care for the mind changed, and what helps people stay well today?

story.title: Two Visits, 180 Years Apart
story.kicker: A student reads a report from the 1840s and then walks into a school clinic.
paragraphs: Maya's history teacher hands out a copy of a document from 1843. It was written by a Massachusetts teacher named Dorothea Dix and presented to the state legislature. Dix had visited jails and poorhouses across the state. She described people with mental illness kept in cages, cellars and stalls, some in chains, some without clothing, in the cold.

Maya reads slowly. Dix did not only complain. She counted, named towns and wrote down what she saw, visit after visit. Her careful evidence persuaded lawmakers to expand a state hospital. She went on to push other states to build hospitals where people could receive care instead of punishment.

After school, Maya walks past her school's wellness room. It has soft light, a couch and a poster with the number 988. Down the hall, the school counselor's door is open. A classmate is inside, talking. Nobody is in chains. Nobody is hidden away. Help is a hallway away.

Maya writes in her notebook: what changed between 1843 and today? New science about the brain. New treatments. New laws. But also new ideas about respect. She realizes the biggest change may be how people talk about minds that work differently or that are going through a hard time.
story.think: Dix used careful evidence to change laws. What kind of evidence could a student gather today to improve mental health support at school?

lessons.title: Dorothea Dix and the Asylums
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1800s, reformers like Dorothea Dix pushed for hospitals that treated mental illness with care, not punishment.
reading: In 1841 Dorothea Dix volunteered to teach a Sunday class at a jail in East Cambridge, Massachusetts. She found people with mental illness held with criminals in an unheated room. She spent the next two years visiting jails and poorhouses. In 1843 she presented her findings, called a *memorial*, to the Massachusetts legislature.

Dix belonged to a reform movement inspired partly by *moral treatment*. This approach, developed by reformers such as Philippe Pinel in France and the Tuke family in England, held that people with mental illness should be treated with kindness, routine, fresh air and useful work. Dix spent decades asking states to build public hospitals based on these ideas.

Many such hospitals, then called *asylums*, opened in the United States in the 1800s. At first, some offered real care. Over time, many became crowded and underfunded. Patients sometimes stayed for decades with little treatment. The story shows a pattern in history: a good reform can fall short when money, staff and attention run out.

words.d: a formal written statement of facts sent to a government to ask for action
a 1700s–1800s approach that treated mental illness with kindness, routine and useful work
an older name for a hospital for people with mental illness

look.title: Dix Speaks to Lawmakers
look.text: I come to call your attention to people with mental illness in this state who are kept in cages, closets, cellars, stalls and pens, chained, unclothed and beaten into obedience.
look.cite: Dorothea Dix, Memorial to the Legislature of Massachusetts, 1843 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Why might Dix list so many specific places? How does this kind of detail persuade lawmakers?

check.q: What did Dorothea Dix find at the East Cambridge jail in 1841?
choices: People with mental illness held with criminals in an unheated room
check.why: Her visit to the jail began her work; she found people with mental illness kept in poor conditions.

check.q: What was moral treatment?
choices: Treating mental illness with kindness, routine and useful work
check.why: Moral treatment, linked with Pinel and the Tukes, stressed kindness, routine and work.

check.q: What happened to many asylums over time?
check.why: The reading says many became crowded, underfunded and offered little treatment.

lessons.title: Leaving the Big Hospitals
lessons.mainIdea: In the late 1900s, care moved from large hospitals to communities, with gains and real gaps.
reading: By the 1950s, hundreds of thousands of Americans lived in state mental hospitals. Then several changes arrived. In the 1950s, the first effective *psychiatric* medicines, such as chlorpromazine, helped many people with severe symptoms. Journalists and courts exposed poor conditions. Many people argued that patients should live in their own communities.

In 1963 President John F. Kennedy signed the Community Mental Health Act. It aimed to build local mental health centers so people could get care near home. Over the next decades, most large hospitals shrank or closed. This shift is called *deinstitutionalization*. Many people gained freedom, jobs and family life they could not have had in a hospital.

But far fewer community centers were built than planned, and funding often fell short. Some people who left hospitals did not get steady care. Many experts link these gaps to people with mental illness who are unhoused or in jails today. Historians and policy experts still debate how much each cause matters. Building strong *community care* remains unfinished work.

words.d: having to do with the medical care of mental illness
moving people out of large mental hospitals into community living and care
mental health services offered close to where people live

look.title: A Promise Half Kept
look.text: Plan: close big hospitals and open many local clinics. Result: most big hospitals closed. Far fewer local clinics opened than planned. Some people thrived at home. Others had nowhere steady to go for care.
look.prompt: Was deinstitutionalization a success, a failure, or both? Support your answer with one fact from each side.

check.q: What did the 1963 Community Mental Health Act aim to do?
choices: Build local mental health centers so people could get care near home
check.why: The act, signed by Kennedy, aimed at local centers for care near home.

check.q: What is deinstitutionalization?
choices: Moving people out of large mental hospitals into community care
check.why: It names the shift from large hospitals to community living and care.

check.q: What was a main gap in deinstitutionalization?
choices: Far fewer community centers were built than planned
check.why: The reading says fewer community centers were built than planned and funding fell short.

lessons.title: Depression and Anxiety
lessons.mainIdea: Depression and anxiety are common, real health conditions, and they are treatable.
reading: Jordan used to love basketball. For the past month he has felt heavy and tired, sleeps badly and has stopped caring about games. Nothing big happened. His friend Ana feels something different. Before tests, her heart races, her stomach knots and worries loop in her head, even when she has studied well. Both are describing real health conditions.

*Depression* is more than a sad day. It is a low mood or loss of interest that lasts at least two weeks and affects sleep, energy, appetite, focus or feelings of worth. An *anxiety disorder* involves fear or worry that is strong, lasts a long time and gets in the way of daily life. Both involve the brain and body, and both are shaped by genes, life events and stress.

These conditions are common. The National Institute of Mental Health estimates that in 2021 about one in five U.S. adults lived with some mental illness. Most important, they are treatable. Many people feel much better with therapy, medication, or both, along with steady routines. If you notice signs like these in yourself or a friend, a trusted adult, school counselor or doctor can help.

words.d: a health condition with low mood or loss of interest lasting at least two weeks
a health condition with strong, lasting fear or worry that gets in the way of daily life
a sign that a person notices, such as poor sleep or a racing heart

look.title: How Common? U.S. Adults, 2021
rows: At least one major depressive episode in the year
look.cite: National Institute of Mental Health, Mental Illness statistics (2021 National Survey on Drug Use and Health)
look.prompt: About how many adults out of 100 lived with any mental illness? What does this suggest about how many people you know may need support?

check.q: How long does low mood usually last to be called depression?
check.why: Depression involves low mood or loss of interest lasting at least two weeks.

check.q: Ana's heart races and worries loop before tests even when she has studied. Which condition fits best?
choices: An anxiety disorder, if it is strong, lasting and gets in the way
check.why: Strong, lasting fear or worry that disrupts life describes an anxiety disorder.

check.q: About what share of U.S. adults lived with any mental illness in 2021, according to NIMH?
check.why: NIMH estimates about 23 percent, roughly one in five.

lessons.title: Talk Therapy and CBT
lessons.mainIdea: Cognitive behavioral therapy helps people notice and change thought patterns, and strong evidence supports it.
reading: Ana tells herself, "If I don't get an A, I'm a failure." Her therapist asks her to write down that thought and look for evidence. Has she ever gotten a B and still done well? Yes. Together they write a more balanced thought: "A B would be disappointing, but I can learn from it." Ana practices this each week.

This method is *cognitive behavioral therapy*, or CBT. It was developed in the 1960s by psychiatrist Aaron Beck at the University of Pennsylvania, building on earlier work. CBT teaches that thoughts, feelings and actions affect one another. By learning to spot unhelpful thoughts and try new actions, people can change how they feel. Therapists often give short practice tasks between sessions.

Many controlled studies show that CBT helps with depression and anxiety disorders. It is often a first choice for young people. It is one kind of *psychotherapy*, or talk therapy. Other kinds focus on relationships, family, or skills for handling strong emotions. A good fit between the person and the *therapist* matters a great deal.

words.d: a talk therapy that helps people notice and change unhelpful thoughts and actions
treatment through talking with a trained professional
a trained professional who provides talk therapy

look.title: Catch the Thought
look.text: Situation: a friend does not answer your text for three hours. Thought: "They must be mad at me." Feeling: worried. Action: you stop texting everyone.
look.prompt: Write a more balanced thought for this situation. How might the feeling and action change?

check.q: Who developed cognitive behavioral therapy in the 1960s?
check.why: Psychiatrist Aaron Beck developed CBT at the University of Pennsylvania.

check.q: What is the core idea of CBT?
choices: Thoughts, feelings and actions affect one another
check.why: CBT teaches that changing thoughts and actions can change feelings.

check.q: What does evidence show about CBT?
choices: It only works for broken bones
Many controlled studies show it helps depression and anxiety
It is banned for young people
check.why: The reading says controlled studies support CBT for depression and anxiety disorders.

lessons.title: Medicine and Daily Habits
lessons.mainIdea: Medication can help some conditions, and sleep, movement and connection support every mind.
reading: Jordan's doctor listens carefully and screens him for depression. She suggests therapy first. After some weeks, they talk about adding medication too. She explains that an *antidepressant* may take several weeks to help, can have side effects, and should never be stopped suddenly without talking to her. Jordan and his parents decide together.

One common group of antidepressants is called *SSRIs*. The first widely used one in the United States, fluoxetine, was approved in 1987. Studies show these medicines help many people with moderate or severe depression and some anxiety disorders. For young people, doctors watch closely, especially in the first weeks. Only a prescriber decides on a medicine and its amount.

Daily habits also matter. Regular *sleep*, physical activity, time outdoors and time with people who care about you support mood and focus. Studies show exercise can ease mild to moderate depression. Habits are not a replacement for treatment when someone needs it. They work best as a steady base alongside therapy or medicine. Tell your doctor about any herbs or supplements, since some can interact with medicines.

words.d: a medicine prescribed to help treat depression and some other conditions
a common group of antidepressant medicines
the body's nightly rest, which supports mood, memory and focus

look.title: Building a Steady Base
look.text: A student's week: bed at 1 a.m. most nights, phone until then, no time outside, lunch alone. Another week: bed by 11, a walk after school, lunch with a friend, and one talk with a counselor.
look.prompt: Which habits in the second week support mental health? Which one would be easiest for you to try first?

check.q: What did Jordan's doctor say about antidepressants?
choices: They may take several weeks, can have side effects, and should not be stopped suddenly
They are safe to share with friends
check.why: The doctor explained the time to work, side effects and not stopping suddenly.

check.q: Who decides whether to use a medicine and how much?
choices: A prescriber, such as a doctor
check.why: Only a prescriber decides on a medicine and its amount.

check.q: How do daily habits fit with treatment?
choices: They replace treatment in all cases
They are a steady base that works alongside therapy or medicine
check.why: The reading says habits support mood and work best alongside treatment when needed.

lessons.title: Addiction and the Brain
lessons.mainIdea: Addiction is a treatable brain condition, not a failure of character.
reading: Picture a man who first took pain pills after back surgery. Over months, he needed more to feel the same effect. When he tried to stop, he felt sick and anxious. He kept using even as it hurt his job and family. His story is common. It shows how a substance can change the brain over time.

*Addiction* is a condition in which a person keeps using a substance or doing an activity despite harm. The National Institute on Drug Abuse describes it as a treatable brain disorder. Many drugs flood the brain's reward system with a chemical messenger called *dopamine*. Over time the brain adapts, and cravings grow. Teen brains are still developing, which is one reason early use carries more risk.

Seeing addiction as a health condition changes how we help. Effective treatment includes counseling and, for opioid addiction, medicines such as buprenorphine and methadone, which have strong evidence. *Recovery* is possible, and many people reach it, sometimes after more than one try. Using respectful words, like "a person with a substance use disorder," makes it easier for people to seek help.

words.d: continuing to use a substance or do an activity despite harm, linked to brain changes
a chemical messenger in the brain's reward system
the process of getting well and building a healthy life after addiction

look.title: Two Ways to Speak
look.text: Headline A: "Addict Arrested Again." Headline B: "Man With Substance Use Disorder Needs Treatment, Family Says." Both headlines describe the same person on the same day.
look.prompt: How might each headline shape what readers think should happen next? Which respects the person more, and why?

check.q: How does the National Institute on Drug Abuse describe addiction?
check.why: NIDA describes addiction as a treatable brain disorder.

check.q: What role does dopamine play in addiction?
choices: It is a medicine for opioid addiction
It is a chemical messenger that drugs flood in the reward system
check.why: Many drugs flood the brain's reward system with dopamine, and the brain adapts.

check.q: Which treatments for opioid addiction have strong evidence?
choices: Medicines such as buprenorphine and methadone, with counseling
check.why: The reading names these medicines, along with counseling, as effective.

lessons.title: How Stigma Is Changing
lessons.mainIdea: Stigma keeps people from seeking help, and open talk from public figures is helping change it.
reading: At the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, gymnast Simone Biles withdrew from several events. She explained that she needed to protect her mental and physical health. Some people criticized her. Many more praised her for being honest. Around the same time, other well-known athletes spoke openly about anxiety and depression.

*Stigma* is a set of negative beliefs and labels attached to a group. For mental health, stigma can sound like "just snap out of it" or jokes about people being "crazy." It can lead people to hide what they are going through. Many people with mental health conditions wait years before seeking help, and stigma is one of the reasons.

Stigma is changing through contact and honest stories. When people hear a friend, teacher or athlete describe a hard time and their recovery, fear drops. Schools add mental health lessons. Words matter too. *Person-first language*, such as "a person with depression," puts the person before the condition. Some people prefer identity-first words; asking is a respectful habit.

words.d: negative beliefs and labels attached to a group that can make people feel ashamed
words that name the person before the condition, like "a person with depression"
choosing to share personal information, such as a health condition, with others

look.title: Rewrite the Line
look.text: Overheard in a hallway: "He's so psycho, he freaked out over a test." "She's just being dramatic, everyone gets sad."
look.prompt: Rewrite each line in a way that is accurate and kind. How might the new words change what the listener does next?

check.q: What is stigma?
choices: Negative beliefs and labels attached to a group
check.why: Stigma is a set of negative beliefs and labels that can shame people.

check.q: How can stigma harm people?
choices: It can lead people to hide their struggles and delay help
check.why: The reading says stigma leads people to hide what they face and wait before seeking help.

check.q: Which is an example of person-first language?
check.why: Person-first language names the person before the condition.

lessons.title: Neurodiversity
lessons.mainIdea: Neurodiversity describes the natural variety of human minds, including autistic people and people with ADHD or dyslexia.
reading: In one classroom, Leo notices patterns in numbers that others miss and prefers a quiet corner. Priya thinks fast, has great ideas and does best when she can move. Sam reads more slowly but tells vivid stories out loud. Each of these students' brains works a little differently. Each has real strengths and specific needs.

The word *neurodiversity* is usually credited to Australian sociologist Judy Singer in the late 1990s. It describes the natural variety in how human brains think, learn and sense the world. People whose brains work in less typical ways, such as autistic people or people with ADHD or dyslexia, are often called *neurodivergent*. The idea encourages respect rather than trying to make everyone the same.

The neurodiversity view does not deny that people may need support. Instead it focuses on *accommodations*, changes that help a person learn or work, such as extra time, quiet spaces, audiobooks or movement breaks. In U.S. public schools, laws such as the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act support plans that fit each student. Many neurodivergent people also value community with others who think like them.

words.d: the natural variety in how human brains think, learn and sense the world
having a brain that works in less typical ways, such as autism, ADHD or dyslexia
a change that helps a person learn or work, such as extra time or a quiet space

look.title: Same Goal, Different Paths
look.text: The assignment: show you understand a chapter. Leo writes a detailed chart. Priya records a two-minute video while walking. Sam listens to the audiobook and explains the chapter out loud to the teacher.
look.prompt: Did all three meet the goal? What accommodations helped each one show what they know?

check.q: Who is usually credited with the word neurodiversity?
check.why: The term is usually credited to Australian sociologist Judy Singer in the late 1990s.

check.q: What does neurodivergent mean?
choices: Having an infection of the brain
Having a brain that works in less typical ways
check.why: Neurodivergent describes brains that work in less typical ways, such as autism, ADHD or dyslexia.

check.q: Which is an accommodation?
check.why: An accommodation is a change that helps, such as extra time or a quiet space.

lessons.title: Mindfulness From Buddhist Roots
lessons.mainIdea: Mindfulness began in Buddhist practice and has been studied as a support for stress, anxiety and depression.
reading: A student sits at her desk before a test. She closes her eyes and notices her breath going in and out. When her mind jumps to worries, she gently brings it back to her breath. After two minutes, her shoulders are lower. She is practicing *mindfulness*: paying attention to the present moment on purpose, without judging it.

Mindfulness has deep roots in Buddhism, which began in ancient India about 2,500 years ago. The Pali word sati, often translated as mindfulness, is part of Buddhist teaching on the path to ending suffering. In Buddhism, *meditation* is a spiritual practice within a larger way of life and ethics.

In 1979, Jon Kabat-Zinn began a program at the University of Massachusetts Medical School called *Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction*. It taught mindfulness in a nonreligious way to patients. A 2014 review in JAMA Internal Medicine found moderate evidence that meditation programs can ease anxiety and depression. They are a helpful tool for many people, not a replacement for treatment when someone needs it.

words.d: paying attention to the present moment on purpose, without judging it
a practice of training attention, often by focusing on the breath
an eight-week program started by Jon Kabat-Zinn in 1979 that teaches mindfulness

look.title: What the Review Found
look.text: Mindfulness meditation programs showed moderate evidence of improving anxiety, depression and pain, and low evidence of improving stress and overall quality of life.
look.cite: Goyal and colleagues, Meditation Programs for Psychological Stress and Well-being, JAMA Internal Medicine, 2014 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: What does "moderate evidence" suggest about how sure scientists are? Why is it important to state the strength of evidence?

check.q: Where does mindfulness have deep roots?
check.why: Mindfulness comes from Buddhist teaching; the Pali word is sati.

check.q: What did Jon Kabat-Zinn start in 1979?
check.why: He began MBSR at the University of Massachusetts Medical School.

check.q: What did the 2014 review find?
choices: Moderate evidence that meditation programs can ease anxiety and depression
check.why: The review found moderate evidence for anxiety, depression and pain.

lessons.title: Mental Health Across Cultures
lessons.mainIdea: Cultures describe distress in different ways, and good care listens to a person's own words and beliefs.
reading: A grandmother tells her doctor that her heart feels heavy and her body aches. She does not use the word depression. In her culture, emotional pain is often described through the body. The doctor listens, asks about sleep, mood and family, and learns she has been grieving since her husband died.

Across the world, people explain and express distress differently. In some cultures, people are more likely to describe body symptoms, such as headaches or tiredness. Many Latin American communities name an *ataque de nervios*, a sudden episode of intense emotion, often after family stress. Traditional Chinese Medicine links emotions with the body's organs and the flow of qi, which is the tradition's own idea.

The American Psychiatric Association's manual, the DSM-5, published in 2013, includes a *Cultural Formulation Interview*. It gives clinicians questions to ask about how a person understands their problem and what help they want. Families, faith leaders and traditional healers may matter a lot. *Culturally responsive care* respects these beliefs while offering treatments that have evidence.

words.d: a term used in many Latin American communities for a sudden episode of intense emotion
a set of questions in the DSM-5 to learn how a person understands their problem
health care that respects a person's culture, language and beliefs

look.title: Asking the Right Questions
look.text: Question A: "Do you have depression?" Question B: "What do you call this problem? What do you think caused it? Who in your life helps when things are hard? What kind of help are you hoping for?"
look.prompt: Which set of questions might help the grandmother most, and why?

check.q: How did the grandmother describe her feelings?
choices: Through her body, like a heavy heart and aches
check.why: In her culture, emotional pain is often described through the body.

check.q: What is the Cultural Formulation Interview?
choices: A set of DSM-5 questions about how a person understands their problem
check.why: It gives clinicians questions about a person's own view of their problem and what help they want.

check.q: What does culturally responsive care do?
choices: Respects a person's beliefs while offering evidence-based treatment
check.why: It honors culture and beliefs while offering treatments with evidence.

lessons.title: 988 and School Supports
lessons.mainIdea: Help is close: 988 is available any time, and schools have trained people ready to listen.
reading: On a night when a friend texts that they feel hopeless, it helps to know what to do. In July 2022 the United States launched *988*, a three-digit number for the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. Anyone can call or text 988, or chat online, any time of day. Trained counselors listen and help people find safety and support. You can also call for a friend.

Schools have supports too. A *school counselor* helps with stress, friendships and plans. School psychologists and social workers can help with learning, emotions and family needs. Many schools use a *safety plan*, a short written list of warning signs, calming steps, people to contact and places to go. In an emergency, call 911.

Helping a friend can be simple. Listen without judging. Take what they say seriously. Stay with them, and tell a trusted adult, even if they asked you to keep it secret. You are not expected to fix everything. Your job is to connect your friend to someone who can help. Reaching out for yourself is also a strong and healthy choice.

words.d: the three-digit number to call or text the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, any time
a trained staff member who helps students with stress, relationships and plans
a short written list of warning signs, calming steps, people to contact and places to go

look.title: Map Your Support
look.text: Draw three circles. Inner circle: people you can talk to any day. Middle circle: adults at school who can help, like a counselor or nurse. Outer circle: help available any time, such as 988 by call or text, and 911 in an emergency.
look.prompt: Who is in each of your circles? If one circle is empty, what is one step you could take to fill it?

check.q: When did the 988 Lifeline number launch?
check.why: The three-digit 988 number launched in July 2022.

check.q: How can a person reach 988?
choices: Call, text or chat, any time
check.why: Anyone can call, text or chat with 988 any time of day.

check.q: A friend says they feel hopeless and asks you to keep it secret. What does the reading say to do?
choices: Keep the secret no matter what
Listen, stay with them and tell a trusted adult
check.why: The reading says to listen, take it seriously, stay with them and tell a trusted adult.

review.q: What did Dorothea Dix use to persuade lawmakers in 1843?
choices: Careful, detailed evidence from her visits
review.why: Dix recorded towns and conditions visit by visit and presented a memorial.

review.q: Put in order: Dix's memorial, the Community Mental Health Act, the 988 launch.
review.why: Dix wrote in 1843, Kennedy signed the Act in 1963, and 988 launched in 2022.

review.q: Which treatment teaches people to spot and change unhelpful thoughts?
review.why: CBT, developed by Aaron Beck, works on thoughts, feelings and actions.

review.q: Which statement about addiction matches the chapter?
choices: It is a treatable brain condition, and recovery is possible
review.why: NIDA describes addiction as a treatable brain disorder; many people recover.

review.q: How does the neurodiversity view approach different minds?
choices: With respect for natural variety and with accommodations
By trying to make everyone the same
review.why: Neurodiversity stresses respect and supports such as accommodations.

review.q: How is modern mindfulness different from its Buddhist roots?
choices: Programs like MBSR teach it in a nonreligious way
review.why: In Buddhism it is part of a spiritual path; MBSR teaches it without religion.

review.q: Why might a doctor use the Cultural Formulation Interview?
choices: To learn how a patient understands their own problem
review.why: It asks how a person understands their problem and what help they want.

review.q: Which is a helpful way to support a friend who is struggling?
choices: Tell them to snap out of it
Listen, take them seriously and connect them with a trusted adult or 988
review.why: The chapter says to listen, stay with them and connect them to help.
